core: Personal data and personally identifiable information (PII): what they are and why aggregation makes them matter
How data is collected: accounts and forms, cookies and pixels/trackers, device fingerprinting, app permissions and advertising identifiers, and location
The data economy: many free services are funded by monetizing user data, usually via targeted advertising
Data brokers: companies that aggregate personal data from many sources into profiles and sell access, largely without consumer knowledge
Trade-offs: convenience and personalization versus exposure
Protective steps: review privacy settings, limit app permissions, use privacy-respecting tools, think before sharing
Privacy laws exist (EU GDPR; U.S. state laws such as California's CCPA/CPRA) framed as educational background, not legal advice
supporting: Tracking can be linked across a user's devices
No single tool or setting guarantees privacy, anonymity, or legal compliance
Data already collected can persist and be sold after a user stops using a service
outOfScope: Digital footprint and online reputation from what a person posts (owned by 'Digital Footprints')
Browser-specific privacy features such as the padlock and private/incognito mode (owned by 'Browsers')
Account security mechanics such as strong passwords and MFA (owned by 'Password Security' and 'Multi-Factor Authentication')
Individualized legal advice on whether a specific privacy law applies to a specific situation
How to build trackers, fingerprinting scripts, or profiling systems

claims.claim: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person and is broad, including names, addresses, email addresses, IP addresses, cookie IDs, phone advertising identifiers, medical records, and identification numbers; personally identifiable information (PII) is the related concept of data that can single out a specific individual.

Websites and apps collect data both directly (accounts and forms) and automatically: sites may set a cookie or use a pixel to identify a device, may use device fingerprinting from a browser's unique configuration, and on phones advertisers may use a unique advertising identifier; activity can also be linked across a user's devices.

A cookie is information saved by a web browser that a site can place to recognize a device on future visits and track a user over time; browser privacy settings and extensions give users some control, and location sharing can be limited.

Data brokers collect personal information from extensive online and offline sources, largely without consumers' knowledge, ranging from purchases and social-media activity to warranty registrations, magazine subscriptions, and religious and political affiliations, combine it into profiles, and sell it for marketing, fraud prevention, and other purposes; the FTC's 2014 study of nine brokers found the industry operates with a fundamental lack of transparency, with brokers collecting billions of data elements covering nearly every U.S. consumer.

Companies track online activity in order to personalize content, serve targeted advertising, and gather analytics, which is the mechanism by which many nominally free services are funded by user data.

Users can reduce (not eliminate) tracking and exposure by adjusting browser and account privacy settings, blocking or limiting cookies, choosing not to share location, deleting cookies or resetting device advertising identifiers, using opt-out tools, and limiting app permissions.

The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since 25 May 2018 and gives individuals rights over their data, including access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, and rights regarding automated decision-making.

California's Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), expanded by the California Privacy Rights Act (effective January 1, 2023), gives California residents rights to know what personal information a business collects, to delete it, to correct it, to opt out of its sale or sharing, and to non-discrimination for exercising those rights.

sourceRecords.title: How Websites and Apps Collect and Use Your Information
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission — Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: FTC consumer guidance. States sites track activity via cookies or pixels and via device fingerprinting (using a browser's unique configuration); phone apps use a unique advertising identifier; activity can be linked across devices. Explains a cookie as information saved by the browser to recognize a device later. Reasons for tracking: save preferences, personalize content, gather analytics, target ads. Protective steps: adjust browser privacy settings, block sites from seeing history, decline location sharing, delete cookies/history, reset phone identifiers, use opt-out tools, review cookie notices. Retrieved via curl with a browser user-agent (WebFetch got HTTP 403). Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Data Brokers: A Call for Transparency and Accountability (FTC Report, May 2014)
sourceRecords.notes: FTC study of nine data brokers. Finds brokers operate with a fundamental lack of transparency; collect and store billions of data elements covering nearly every U.S. consumer from extensive online and offline sources, largely without consumers' knowledge (purchases, social-media activity, warranty registrations, magazine subscriptions, religious and political affiliations); combine into profiles and sell for marketing, fraud prevention, and other purposes. Quantitative detail: one broker held information on more than 1.4 billion consumer transactions and 700 billion data elements; another adds more than 3 billion data points per month. Facts read from the FTC press release (ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2014/05/ftc-recommends-congress-require-data-broker-industry-be-more-transparent-give-consumers-greater), retrieved via curl; report landing page registered as canonical URL. Used as dated 2014 figures.

sourceRecords.title: Data protection explained
sourceRecords.notes: Official EU explainer. Defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual, with examples including names, addresses, email addresses, IP addresses, cookie IDs, medical records, identification numbers, and phone advertising identifiers; irreversibly anonymized data is not personal data. Lists the GDPR as the EU's main data-protection law and enumerates eight individual rights (information, access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, automated-decision-making). Reference-only; facts stated in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: General data protection regulation (GDPR) — summary
sourceRecords.provider: EUR-Lex (Publications Office of the European Union)
sourceRecords.notes: Official EUR-Lex summary of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. Confirms the GDPR was adopted 27 April 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. Used only to anchor the application date. Reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
sourceRecords.provider: California Office of the Attorney General
sourceRecords.notes: California Attorney General's CCPA page. States CCPA rights: to know what personal information a business collects and how it is used, to delete personal information (with exceptions), to opt out of sale/sharing, and to non-discrimination; the CPRA (Prop 24, effective January 1, 2023) added rights to correct and to limit use of sensitive personal information. Defines personal information as data that identifies, relates to, or could reasonably be linked with a person or household. Reference-only; stated in original wording.
